abstract: Our second visual benchmark goes from tissue to single cells.

metadata.author: Ian Ferenc Diks

content.value:
CellMicroscopyBench is our second benchmark that focuses mainly on the visual capabilities of AI agents. This time we go one scale down, from tissue to single cells and the structures inside them. Some of the imaging is familiar from tissue, like fluorescence, only at another scale. Some of it is new, with different physics behind it, like cryo-electron tomograms and nanometer-scale localization data. At this scale much of the work is no longer recognizing a structure that is in plain view but deciding what in the image is the object at all.

The benchmark contains 26 tasks from eight publicly available datasets, and each task is run in triplicate across every model-harness combination. The highest pass rate was 23.1%, reached by both GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.2 Astra on the Pi harness.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Most important facts

  • Agents find cell microscopy tasks very hard. Across 2,496 total runs, only 10.5% passed (262 runs). 16 of 26 tasks were not solved by any combination.

  • OpenAI’s GPT models performed the best. GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.2 Astra on the Pi harness tied for the top spot with a pass rate of 23.1%. This was followed by GPT-6.2 Sol on Pi at 21.8%. GPT-6.2 Sol cost about $1 per run, which was about five times less costly than the other top configurations (about $5 to $6 per run).

  • Performance varied by task type. Agents did best at counting and timing clear events in fluorescence images, such as finding damaged nuclei or spotting when a cell divides (57%). They struggled with faint or fine structures, like membranes in cryo-electron tomograms (3 of 672 runs) and oocyte nuclei in brightfield (1 of 480). Agents also struggled with telling real events from look-alikes in long movies, such as cell deaths and ERK signaling waves, which were never solved.

Why Cell Microscopy

Much of cell biology was worked out by looking at single cells. Measurements over a whole population average away what each cell does. When cells are treated with an antimitotic drug (e.g., paclitaxel), some die during mitotic arrest while others slip out of mitosis without dividing and survive. Imaging is one of the simplest and most established ways to acquire this information quickly and at high quality.

These images are not scarce. Modern microscopes image thousands of samples in a single run, and public repositories hold a large body of experiments that were analyzed once for a scientific question and rarely revisited. AI agents could help get more out of this data, but only if their reports can be trusted.

So we wanted to know how far frontier models actually get on real cell images. Every task in CellMicroscopyBench starts from raw data and ends in a scientific answer that we can check (similar to TissueMicroscopyBench).

The Leaderboard

We assessed 32 configurations of 24 models under three harnesses (Pi, Claude Code, and Grok build). Each configuration attempted three runs per task. 131 runs did not produce a gradeable answer because of errors, timeouts, or malformatted responses. That leaves 2,365 graded runs, of which 11.1% passed overall. OpenAI models performed best: GPT-6 Astra (Pi) and GPT-6.2 Astra (Pi) both passed 23.1% of runs, followed by GPT-6.2 Sol (Pi) at 21.8%. Claude Opus 5.5 (Claude Code) was the strongest non-OpenAI configuration at 20.5%. The top nine configurations, which include Gemini 4 Carbon and Neon and Claude Fable 5.2, are within four passes of each other, which is within run-to-run noise.

Cost varied far more than performance. GPT-6.2 Sol reached near-top accuracy at a median of about $1 per run, against $8 for Opus 5.5 and $24 for Fable 5.2. The choice of harness didn’t have a huge impact. The same model scored within two passes across harnesses, unless one harness caused more crashes.

The tasks were designed to be challenging. 10 of the 26 tasks were solved by at least one configuration, while 16 were never solved. Performance depended strongly on the type of the task. Agents did best on counting and timing events in fluorescence data, such as picking DNA-damaged nuclei or finding the exact frame of anaphase onset (57% each). Cryo-electron tomography was rarely solved: 3 passes in 672 runs. Brightfield tasks that require tracing the faint nuclear boundary of an oocyte passed once in 480 runs.

Benchmark design

We built 26 tasks on eight public datasets. Agents are asked to analyze cryo-electron tomograms of autophagosome formation in yeast and of ER exit sites, confocal 3D stacks of lipid transport and nuclear shape, transmitted-light movies of oocyte maturation, time-lapse recordings of dividing cells, live-cell biosensor movies of ERK signaling waves, and 3D MINFLUX localizations of nuclear pores. The tasks span membrane and organelle ultrastructure, 3D reconstruction, and measurements of cells and nuclei, event detection in time-lapse, and classification of cell states, with most of them focused on reconstructing structures.

In each task, agents receive the raw images and have to come back with a polygon outline, a 3D volume, a set of events with their frame and positions or measurements in physical units, or an ordering. We compare the agent outputs with an expert annotation of the same data. We also had experts verify a subset of our hardest tasks to prove solvability. When a task failed human expert verification, we revised the task to ensure it was fair and scientifically sound.

Many of the cell microscopy tasks cannot be fixed into specific computational rules. We designed tasks around this notion and around agents needing to visually inspect and analyze the images. Examples are separating the faint nuclear envelope from the bright nucleolus inside it, deciding whether a borderline spindle counts as aligned, or identifying which coat protein surrounds a vesicle in a low-contrast tomogram. Agents might be able to narrow down candidates using code, but the agent must look at the images to make the correct call.

Analysis scope

Cell division, meiosis, and spindle orientation

These tasks ask what happens when and where in a movie of dividing cells. When the answer is one clear moment, agents do well. 55 of 96 runs found the exact frame in which the cells start to separate their chromosomes.

It gets much harder once the answer needs every cell that fits a description. In one task the agent has to mark all cells whose spindle has lined up. About half of the runs (47 of 96) came back with the same number of cells, mostly the same ones, and three of the cells we were looking for were each missed by more than three quarters of the runs. No run passed this task.

Membrane remodeling and organelle contacts on cryo-ET

Most of these tasks ask the agent to rebuild a structure from a cryo-electron tomogram as a 3D volume by outlining it on plane after plane. A tomogram is a grey, noisy volume where membranes are thin dark lines. Across the six tasks, only 2.5% of runs passed, and none of the five autophagy tasks was ever solved.

When agents find the right structure, they tend to get fairly close. In the example below, three agents rebuild the same phagophore, the membrane sac that forms during autophagy. They go about it quite differently, one with 23 outlines and another with 138, and they all end up with a similar shape, but none of them follows the membrane closely enough to pass.

Three agents rebuild the same phagophore, next to the reference. The shapes look alike, but the sizes differ more than the video suggests: Gemini 4 Neon’s volume is about 3% larger than the references’ tolerance. Claude Fable 5.2’s about 14% smaller, and GPT-6.2 Astra’s about a third larger.

The other way these tasks go wrong is less subtle. In 28 of the 72 scored answers on this task, the agent outlined something that does not even overlap with the structure we asked for. In the run below, Opus 5.5 carefully traces the membranes of a neighboring mitochondrion instead. The tracing itself is good, it’s just the wrong object.

Conclusion

Inside cells, agents are fairly good at saying when one clear thing happens and much weaker at saying exactly where a structure is, especially in 3D. They often find the right structure and still don’t follow its borders closely enough, and sometimes they put the same careful work into the wrong object. Finding every cell that fits a description in a crowded movie stays hard as well. These aren’t questions where analysis based on thresholding would get you to the answer, and for now it appears that agents still lack this specific ability.

What changes from tissue is the scale, and with it how much of the object the image shows. Tissue also had fluorescence, but there, a structure spans many cells and is mostly in plain view. Thus, the work is to recognize and draw a line around it. Inside a single cell the object is often at the edge of what the recording can show, and each modality hides it in its own way. In fluorescence a bright signal can overshadow the object itself. In cryo-electron tomograms the signal-to-noise ratio is much lower, and artifacts can look like signal where there is none. So these tasks are not simply about looking at a picture and comparing objects. First, the agent has to judge what is signal at all. These are subtle things, and it fits what we saw: the tasks on the images with the least contrast were the ones that were rarely solved.

CellMicroscopyBench covers a focused subset of cell microscopy for now, and we plan to keep expanding and maintaining it alongside TissueMicroscopyBench. We hope that it becomes a useful resource for cell biologists and microscopists deciding where to trust an agent and for model developers deciding on where to improve.
